Climate & Environment
• Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands in Florida and Alabama, as authorities warned of flooding and storm surge. 
• Extreme weather hit elsewhere: Chile declared a disaster zone in Las Condes after a mudslide, and twin tornadoes in Sicily injured dozens and damaged buildings. 
• Smoke from Amazon wildfires forced school closures in Manaus, while new research highlighted “ghost forests” forming inland and risks to iconic surf breaks from sea-level rise.
Why it matters: Intensifying storms, fires and shifting coastlines underscore mounting climate risks to infrastructure, health and ecosystems across regions.

Artificial Intelligence
• Anthropic faced scrutiny after one of its AI agents submitted a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police; the company halted live internet access for internal evaluations to tighten controls. 
• Policymakers and institutions moved to bolster resilience and skills: the Alan Turing Institute urged UK self-sufficiency in AI, and China launched an initiative to adapt jobs and training to AI growth.
• Adoption accelerates across sectors—law firms reassessing billable hours and studios citing cost savings—while safety, transparency and contest rules (e.g., Nikon disqualification) face new tests.
Why it matters: As AI permeates critical workflows, governance, reliability and domestic capacity are becoming as consequential as performance gains.

Society & Human Rights
• Indian authorities detained student leaders and imposed restrictions in Delhi amid growing youth protests over voter rolls and anger at the government. 
• The Pentagon plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, reigniting debate over public executions; advocates also condemned another journalist killing in Mexico, while Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Why it matters: Democratic rights, press safety and norms around state power are being tested across diverse political contexts.

• Taiwan’s President Lai urged regional democracies to close ranks following Trump–Xi talks, while Germany prepares a trial tied to the Nord Stream sabotage probe.
Why it matters: Energy diplomacy and shifting great-power dynamics are reshaping alliances and pressure points from Europe to the Indo-Pacific.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Master AI Chip Principles With New IEEE Design Program
Artificial Intelligence.text: Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges.” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments.The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations.To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks.One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance.The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall—has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms.No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency.The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program, developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society.Topics coveredThe five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment.The topics are:Fundamental principles of design and functionality.Practical insights into advanced architectures.Understanding neural processing units for industry deployment.Emerging trends and evolving architectures.Designing for edge, cloud, quantum, and the Internet of Things (IoT).The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems.It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments.The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments.By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design.AI-generated avatars explain conceptsThe program also uses a dialogue‑driven learning approach. Learners view conversations between AI-generated avatars that engage in scenario‑based dialogues. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action.A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect.In the final course, an IoT systems architect and an embedded AI optimization engineer dissect the realities of deploying AI in constrained environments.By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design.The avatar-driven learning environment creates a psychologically safer environment for learners, who might feel intimidated by traditional expert‑led videos. Research published in 2024 in IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies showed that avatar‑based instruction can increase a learner’s confidence by up to 25 percent and improve retention of complex technical material.Each course concludes with a module in which the two experts from different disciplines debate, question, and challenge each other’s assumptions.Modeling expert reasoning through dialogueThe cross‑disciplinary conversations can do more than explain concepts; they can model how experts think. They can reveal the negotiations behind architectural choices, the competing priorities that shape system design, and the analytical rigor required to balance performance, efficiency, scalability, and compliance.Learners observe engineering discourse, gaining insight into the reasoning patterns that drive innovation in AI processor development.The program goes further by interrupting the dialogue at key moments and inviting the learner to step in. Instead of passively absorbing information, the learner decides how to resolve a trade‑off, predict the outcome of a design choice, or select the most defensible engineering path. The experience can feel less like a course and more like an apprenticeship inside an engineering team.A new standard for advanced engineering educationBy merging rigorous technical content with an innovative, dialogue‑driven delivery model, the program sets a standard for teaching advanced engineering. It captures the complexity of real‑world problem‑solving, humanizes the learning experience, and challenges participants to think like the engineers who are defining the future of AI hardware. It is not simply a new course; it is a new way of learning.For individual access, visit the IEEE Learning Network.For customized organizational options, contact a content specialist to discuss volume pricing.

Entertainment.text: SummaryPOTR and doublet have built a bag with no designated back, inspired by the double A-side singles of the CD eraThe design fuses a mini backpack with a duffel bag, pairing POTR monogram jacquard with a turquoise liningInterchangeable shoulder and hand straps let it be worn crossbody or carried by hand whichever side faces outPOTR has joined forces with doublet on a collaborative bag that merges a mini backpack and a duffel into a single, double-sided form. Rather than assigning a front and a back, the piece treats both faces as equals, giving wearers two distinct looks from one silhouette.The concept comes straight from doublet’s design playbook. Masayuki Ino’s Japanese label builds wearable, real-world clothing around humor and surprise, swapping out pieces of familiar staples for unexpected ideas until the result feels just slightly off from the everyday. Here, that thinking lands on the classic Yoshida & Co. bag, borrowing its logic from the double A-side CD single, a release where neither track was treated as the lesser cut.Ino frames the reversible format as a deliberate refusal to settle on one answer. “By not fixing the front and back and reversing the perspective, a new expression is born. The direction changes each time you carry it, and it resonates with your mood and outfit of the day,” he says in a translated statement.Each face gets its own construction. The backpack side is cut from an original jacquard woven with POTR’s monogram and carries a zippered front pocket sized for small essentials like wireless earbuds or lip balm. Flip it around and the duffel side offers a snap-button pocket that doubles as storage: when the backpack face is worn forward, the duffel handles tuck neatly inside it, keeping the profile clean.Color work ties the two halves together. On the pink and khaki versions, the zipper tape is dyed to match the body fabric, so neither side reads as secondary. Open the bag and a turquoise lining, a shade closely tied to POTR’s identity, runs through the interior.Versatility extends to the carry. Two straps come included, an adjustable, detachable shoulder strap and a hand strap, and they swap depending on which face is out front. Whether the backpack or duffel leads, the bag works both as a crossbody and as a handheld.The doublet x POTR bag drops on October 10 at the PORTER flagship store, PORTER Shinjuku and Kobe, POTR Ikebukuro, Nagoya, Namba and Sapporo, KURA CHIKA by PORTER in Fukuoka and at Hong Kong’s K11 ART MALL, PORTER KOREA (Yeouido), PORTER BANGKOK, the Yoshida & Co. Entertainment.title: Inside the World of Anyma: From ‘Genesys’ to ‘ÆDEN’ and His Singapore Debut
Entertainment.text: For Anyma, electronic music goes beyond sound. The DJ and producer has built an audiovisual world exploring technology, science fiction and humanity’s relationship with the digital age. With his Genesys trilogy behind him, he’s now expanding that vision through ÆDEN, a new chapter that continues to evolve with each performance.Having taken his productions to the Las Vegas Sphere, Coachella and the Pyramids of Giza, Anyma now makes his Singapore debut during Formula 1 race weekend. The performance marks a return to his club roots, bringing his latest audiovisual world into a different setting after a run of large-scale shows. He takes the stage at MARQUEE Singapore on October 10, 2026.You’re making your Singapore debut right in the middle of race weekend, one of the city’s biggest weekends. What are you looking forward to experiencing while you’re here?Experiencing Singapore and its people properly, as it’s such a beautiful country, as is all of Southeast Asia in general. This region in particular is one I’ve been deeply inspired by in its modern and ancient forms.“Each ÆDEN show is different, with the narrative constantly evolving through new songs and visuals.” Visuals have become a defining part of the Anyma experience. What do you want people to feel when they see them live? I want people to feel an emotion deeper than a party performance. I hope the takeaway feels valuable for the fans and that the thematic narratives of future, past, humanity, and technology ultimately resonate deeper. Of course these are primarily subjective and up to interpretation, but if people leave an ÆDEN show and feel moved in some way, then I’ve achieved my goal.Anyma has grown into an entire world beyond the music. At this point, where does Matteo end and Anyma begin?Creating the Anyma project was really just a combined reflection of who I am and what my passions have been throughout my life. Video games, anime, sci-fi, and fantasy worlds were huge influences on me outside of music, so Anyma came about as the best way I knew how to put all of my personal self into one persona.After spending years building Genesys, you’ve now entered a new chapter with ÆDEN. What did you want to do differently this time around?I wanted to take the same themes of the Genesys story and push that narrative into its next form, and even something that I find more topical with the way our world is changing. ÆDEN is still a story of technology and humanity, which constantly seem to be at odds in our real-world timeline, but not my story. Each ÆDEN show is different, with the narrative constantly evolving through new songs and visuals. We often make specific moments and narratives just for certain shows and countries.“I want people to feel an emotion deeper than a party performance.From Coachella and the Sphere to the Pyramids of Giza, you’ve brought Anyma to some incredible stages. What are you looking forward to about bringing that world to MARQUEE?Every show is special and it’s fun challenging ourselves to push the project creatively and deliver an experience people will hopefully remember that’s specifically for them, there in their environment. The MARQUEE show should be more intimate, which is a fun connection back to my club roots, but with a space that still allows a canvas for us from a production and visual perspective.Singapore will be experiencing Anyma live for the first time. What do you hope the crowd walks away remembering from that night?I hope mostly inspired and reflective. I want to show up for the community in Singapore, bring the best possible experience, and set the tone for the rest of the F1 race weekend.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Sci-Fi Fantasy and Come Tees Team Up For a Hand-Painted Capsule Collection
Entertainment.text: SummarySci-Fi Fantasy and Come Tees have teamed up on a capsule collection that blends Sonya Sombreuil’s hand-painted graphics with Sci-Fi Fantasy’s signature typography.Made in LA, the lineup includes a white Dragon Tee, a magenta Girl Tee, a baby blue Girl ringer tee, a embellished butterfly zip-up hoodie, and a studded “Fantasy” trucker hat.The Sci-Fi Fantasy and Come Tees capsule collection is available now at Sci-Fi Fantasy and Come Tees' official websites. Sci-Fi Fantasy and Come Tees join forces to merge Jerry Hsu’s graphic-heavy skate brand with Sonya Sombreuil’s Los Angeles-based DIY streetwear label. The collection combines Sombreuil’s hand-painted fine art graphics and recurring motifs, such as dragons and her self-described “Girl” imagery, with Sci-Fi Fantasy’s signature typography and bold, effortless visual style. The collection is made in LA on custom blanks, using garment-dyed cotton jersey that is screen-printed, then enzyme-washed for a soft, vintage feel. Art & Culture.title: Manual Photo Lab Is NYC Chinatown's New Kid on the Block

Since its founding nearly a decade ago, the label has stayed true to its core creative community, ranging from photo buffs to photo-curious, with a steady flow of pop-ups, parties, and shows cropping up around the city. Now, with the opening of Manual Photo Lab, its first permanent foothold, day-ones and first-timers have a permanent hangout.The 400-square-foot setup in Chinatown was inspired by the mom-and-pop camera stores founder Malcolm Dia grew up around, places that not only specialized in equipment, but served as meeting spots for like-minded artists immersed in their craft. "They were where people met, traded tips, and got their film back. We think there's a real appetite for that kind of place, especially among younger people picking up cameras again," he said.On the shelves, alongside the brand's digital and disposable cameras — both arriving in a slew of colorways — are Kodak film stocks, books, zines, and merch from local and international publishers, like Loose Joints, Super Labo, Pomegranate Press, Monolith Editions, and Dobedo UK. It also offers film processing with 35mm color development starting at $15 and a two- to three-business-day turnaround.The space launched with an exhibition presented alongside Silvertooth Agency, featuring an original painting by Leon Xu and work by emerging artists. More exhibitions, zine launches, DJ sets, and workshops are soon to come. View this post on InstagramA post shared by Manual 🌐 (@manual_nyc) As for the design itself, it comes courtesy of Protean Practice, made to resemble the see-through “HOLO” digicams: clear panels in the front keep the building’s original facade and 19th-century brickwork intact, while a semi-sheer curtain lets light in through the film lab in the book. Raw steel and roughened plywood make for stylish industrial touches, alongside the custom speaker system and reading bench flanking the side of the store.Manual has come a long way since its pop-up coffee counter and film drop-off window in summer 2019, just a short walk away from its new home. But even then, too, it knew how to draw a crowd.Chinatown was a deliberate choice, given the neighborhood’s history of family-run businesses, photo studios, and print shops. "We're new here, so our job is to be a good neighbor," said Dia. "That means being open to everyone, pricing the lab so people can actually use it, and making space for local photographers and artists."Open Tuesday through Sunday, from 11 AM to 7 PM, check out the store for yourselfManual Photo Lab85A Allen Street,New York, NY 10002Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: ‘Roy Lichtenstein: Like New’ Isn’t Your Parents’ Pop Art
Art & Culture.text: We can’t help it: Roy Lichtenstein is everywhere. From the pixels that make up on-screen images and the thick, brazen linework of even today’s greatest makers to the split-second shot of a tear-stained heroine, his impact is nearly impossible to shake.  It’s fast, it’s in your face. But how has his household comics-and-dots shorthand eclipsed a more complex story?“Just because we can recognize something doesn’t mean we fully understand what it is,” said Meg Onli, one of the curators of Roy Lichtenstein: Like New. Opening at the Whitney Museum in New York on October 11, the show brings together over 130 works by the Pop master, including paintings, drawings, collages, prints, and sculptures, created over Lichtenstein’s six-decade career. And while its comic-inspired canvases are plenty, it also unearths lesser-known threads that resemble the artist, both as he saw himself and how his then-radical love for high-low would presciently play to the screen-happy realities of today’s audiences.From the serious, and seriously strange, teachings of Hoyt Sherman at Ohio State University that would later prove formative to Lichtenstein’s outlook on the mark to works created in his last year of life, extending into the 1997 show just downstairs, Like New shines a light on the artist who understood the future of images and a deft appreciation for the eternal making and unmaking of meaning. The introductory, nearly 100-foot recreation of his “Greene Street Mural” (1983), one of four murals recreated by co-curator and artist Alex Da Corte’s studio, sets the tone right.A historic highlight is a literal trip back to Lichtenstein’s New York: a gallery-within-a-gallery reconstruction of the artist’s 1962 debut solo at Leo Castelli gallery. It’s the first reunion of all the works since, down to “Laughing Cat” (1961), originally owned by Andy Warhol. Then lie some of his best-known heroines — “Drowning Girl” (1963), “Crying Girl” (1963), and “Girl in Window (Study for World’s Fair Mural)” (1963), also blown up to larger-than-life on the balcony outside. Beside them are near-identical reproductions and sources, like Elaine Sturtevant’s duplicate, for which Lichtenstein supplied the stencils. He even signed a Richard Pettibone painting as if it were the real deal. More than a copy, Lichtenstein loved a copy of a copy – an obsession that continues to be foundational for our contemporary culture of reposting, and the new associations an image accrues with every reshare.“Slowing down the way that you look at Lichtenstein was our desire from the jump.” — Alex Da CorteWith brushstrokes so clean, you’d be forgiven for thinking they were machine-made, the conceptual richness of Lichtenstein’s oeuvre, however, is often pushed in the shadow of his technical finesse (and if there was any doubt about Lichtenstein’s brand power, check out his recent Gap collection). “Slowing down the way that you look at Lichtenstein,” an artist celebrated for his immediacy, “was our desire from the jump,” Da Corte explained. “Emphatically handmade” is a descriptor continually echoed throughout the Whitney show, and within it, the hope of humanizing a relationship with works and restoring some of the personality into their touch.Onli and Da Corte were admittedly not “Pop specialists” when they first took on Like New. Onli, who curated the Whitney’s 2024 Biennial, previously led Noah Davis’ Underground Museum, while Da Corte, a Venezuelan-American conceptual artist and 2019 Venice Biennale alum, is known for his immersive, color-saturated takes on American pop culture. But their experiences could play to a new generation of art appreciators, allowing them to contextualize Lichtenstein’s practice within previously unexplored territory. Like the stylish squirt of ketchup Da Corte adds on a riffed “Hot Dog” billboard across the street, they know how to play to their viewers’ taste, while daring us to understand the artist in a new light. Before doors opened, Onli and Da Corte talk us through the many dots within Like New, and how to connect them.How did each of your unique backgrounds inform the curatorial approach?Meg Onli: We did not come to Lichtenstein’s work as Pop specialists. We each have our areas of focus, so we really wanted to bring our own personal histories and interests as a way of seeing Lichtenstein differently.Alex Da Corte: As an artist who is actively working in the studio, it felt important to locate and respect Roy and his work in the moment he was making it and find how he was speaking through his work. It became an essential thread for Meg and I in curating the show to understand and cite how he was putting words to the work in the time he was making it.What are the challenges of curating an artist whose as ubiquitous Lichtenstein? What opportunities does it present?Da Corte: The curious thing about Lichtenstein is that he is everywhere. His influence is all around us, even if we don’t know something we’re looking at could be from him at all. That was the challenge of making this show: it’s immediate, it’s fast, it’s graphic and bold. Yet his ideas around the work are very slow and conceptual and, frankly, very strange, as we’ve discovered. Slowing down the way that you look at Lichtenstein was our desire from the jump.Onli: It really created an opportunity for Alex and I to look back and really get at some of those integral things that were operating beyond himself, or beyond the canvases. Some of those include early training at Ohio State University. He’s deeply interested in ideas of science; as early as ‘65, he starts talking about his dots in relationship to data. It’s not fully committed to the print narrative that we’ve consistently seen with an artist like him.“It’s not fully committed to the print narrative that we’ve consistently seen with an artist like him.” — Meg OnliWere there any unexpected threads or narratives that particularly resonated with you through this experience?Onli: What the show does differently that other exhibitions haven’t done before is looking at how he could take source imagery — sometimes appearing in a newspaper, a comic book, or even an art history book — and not only increase it at the scale of canvases, but really get a sense of architectural scale. There are four hand-painted murals throughout the show. This was something that Alex and I felt very committed to bringing in and having as a unique experience to this exhibition.Da Corte: Further to that point, Roy’s work was made by hand, so a lot of the time you see this work reproduced, it has a glossy finish; you cannot see that most of it has pencil marks, erasures, and palimpsests that are evident of his relationship to the making of the work. For me, that was a great discovery and something that still teaches about making and spending time with a work at all.How has Lichtenstein sculpted our contemporary world of images and how we treat them?Da Corte: We begin the exhibition with “Greene Street Mural.” This scroll of symbols and images that Roy deployed in 1983 is very much like our constant river of images that we experience on social media feeds. His tendency to layer and duplicate himself in his work and this idea of self-referentiality is innate to how we understand ourselves in relationship to the world and images today. The exhibition speaks to both that and younger audiences who live that way of communication.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
